docs.title: ridegraph.graph
docs.text:
Road network storage and the weighted routing graph built from it.

Two layers, kept separate on purpose:

  • RoadNetwork is the raw map: where nodes are, which segments join them, how long each segment is and what kind of road it is. It is what the data pipeline produces and what gets saved to disk.
  • Graph is what algorithms run on: a compact directed graph whose edge weights are travel times. Changing the cost model (traffic, time of day) means building a new Graph from the same RoadNetwork.

Edges are stored in CSR (compressed sparse row) form: all outgoing edges of node u live in head[first_out[u]:first_out[u + 1]]. It is the layout production routing engines use, being cache friendly and trivially serialised.

docs.title: ridegraph.dijkstra
docs.text:
Dijkstra's algorithm: the correctness baseline every faster method is tested against.

It grows a ball of settled nodes around the source in order of travel time, so by the time the target is settled its time is provably optimal. The cost is that the ball covers everything closer than the target in every direction, which is exactly the waste A* and Contraction Hierarchies remove.

Implementation notes:

  • Binary heap with lazy deletion. Instead of a decrease-key operation, a better distance is simply pushed again and stale entries are skipped when popped. In Python this beats any hand-rolled indexed heap.
  • Distances live in a dict touched only for reached nodes, so a short query on a big graph does not pay to initialise an array of every node.

docs.title: ridegraph.ch
docs.text: Contraction Hierarchies: the preprocessing trick behind production routing engines.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
Rank every node by "importance", then remove (contract) them one at a time, least important first. Removing node v can break quickest routes that pass through it, so for each neighbour pair u -> v -> w we check whether some other route from u to w is at least as quick (a witness). If not, we add a shortcut edge u -> w with the combined cost and remember it skips v.

After all nodes are contracted, every quickest route in the original graph has an equivalent route in the augmented graph that only goes up the ranking from the source and then only down the ranking into the target. A query is therefore a bidirectional Dijkstra in which each side may only climb. Each side sees a tiny "upward cone" of the graph instead of a ball of the city, which is where the orders-of-magnitude speedup comes from.

docs.title: Implementation choices
docs.text:
• Node order by lazy priority updates: priority is the edge difference (shortcuts added minus edges removed) plus the number of already-contracted neighbours, which spreads contraction evenly across the map. A node's priority is recomputed when it reaches the top of the queue; if it is no longer the minimum it goes back in.
  • Witness search is a local Dijkstra capped by cost and settled count. If the cap is hit we add the shortcut anyway: an unneeded shortcut costs a little space, never correctness.
  • Stall-on-demand at query time: if a node can be reached more cheaply through a higher-ranked node the search has already seen, its upward distance is provably not optimal and its edges are not expanded.
  • Path unpacking: each shortcut stores its middle node, so a route of shortcuts expands recursively back into real road segments.

up_* arrays hold, for each node u, edges u -> v to higher-ranked nodes. down_* arrays hold, for each node v, edges u -> v from higher-ranked nodes, indexed at v so the backward search can climb from the target.

docs.title: many_to_many(sources, targets, buckets=None)
docs.text:
Travel time from every source to every target (inf if unreachable).

Bucket-based many-to-many (Knopp et al., 2007): one backward upward search per target files its distances in buckets at the nodes it reaches; one forward upward search per source then reads the buckets of the nodes it reaches. Cost grows with sources + targets, not their product, which is what lets a dispatcher price every driver against every waiting rider at once. Reuse buckets when targets repeat.

docs.title: ridegraph.cch
docs.text:
Customizable Contraction Hierarchies: preprocessing once, new traffic in milliseconds.

Ordinary Contraction Hierarchies (ch.py) choose which shortcuts to add by running witness searches with the current travel times. Change the times (a closure, a jam) and the whole hierarchy is stale. Customizable CH (Dibbelt, Strasser and Wagner, 2016) splits the work in three:

  1. Metric-independent preprocessing (slow, once per map). Order the junctions by nested dissection: cut the city in two along a thin separator, order each half recursively, and put the separator last. Then contract in that order without witness searches: every pair of higher neighbours gets a shortcut. The result is a fixed "chordal" graph whose size does not depend on travel times.
  2. Customization (fast, whenever times change). Give every original road its current time, then sweep the lower triangles bottom-up: for a shortcut u-w over a lower junction v, u->w = min(u->w, u->v + v->w). Every shortcut now holds the true quickest time between its ends using only lower junctions, which is exactly what the CH query needs.
  3. Queries as in CH: two upward searches meeting at the top.

Because step 1 never looks at travel times, the separators come from the road layout alone: a geometric cut picks the direction (north-south, east-west or a diagonal) that crosses the fewest roads, the way rivers and parks make natural cuts in a real city.

docs.title: ridegraph.alternatives
docs.text:
Alternative routes: a few genuinely different ways to make the same trip.

A map app that shows only the quickest route hides useful choices: a route a minute slower that avoids a charge, or stays on main roads. Good alternatives must be (Abraham et al., "Alternative routes in road networks"):

  • different: share at most max_overlap of their length with any route already offered;
  • not much slower: at most max_stretch times the quickest;
  • sensible: no pointless detours.

This module uses the penalty method: find the quickest route, make every road on it a little slower, search again, and repeat. Each search is pushed off the roads already used, so it finds the next most natural corridor. Candidates are judged on the real travel times, not the penalised ones. A detour check then rejects candidates that leave a road only to rejoin it: every short stretch of the route must be close to the quickest way between its ends.

The same machinery avoids an area: roads into it cost infinity, so every route found keeps out. That is how the Congestion Charge zone is avoided.

docs.title: ridegraph.live
docs.text:
Live road disruptions from Transport for London, matched onto the graph.

TfL's open Unified API lists current roadworks, closures and incidents on London's streets, each as a polyline with a severity and a closure state (/Road/all/Street/Disruption). This module

  1. fetches and parses that feed (standard library only, no key needed for light use),
  2. map-matches each disrupted stretch onto graph edges: an edge is on the stretch when both its ends and its midpoint lie within MATCH_M metres of the polyline, and
  3. turns the result into a time multiplier per edge: infinity for a closed road, a slowdown for the rest by severity.

The multipliers are applied to the time-of-day weights, and a Customizable Contraction Hierarchy (cch.py) re-customises in milliseconds, so the quickest-route queries stay instant with live closures in force.

docs.title: ridegraph.reach
docs.text:
Travel-time maps: everywhere reachable within a time budget.

An isochrone answers "where can I get to in 20 minutes from here?" (or, for someone choosing where to live, "from where can I get to my office in 20 minutes?"). It is a single-source search that settles every junction in time order and stops at the budget, so it touches only the reachable part of the city. Run on the reverse graph, the same search measures journeys into a point.

Reachable area is reported by counting 250 m squares that contain a reached junction, which tracks what a map reader sees better than a convex hull would around a river or a park.

docs.title: ridegraph.tour
docs.text:
Multi-stop routes: the best order to visit a list of addresses.

A courier with a van and ten drops wants the order that gets them all done soonest: the travelling salesman problem, on real one-way streets, so the time from A to B is not the time from B to A. The pipeline:

  1. One matrix of travel times. A many-to-many Contraction Hierarchies query prices every stop against every other stop at the chosen time of day.
  2. Exact for small jobs. Held-Karp dynamic programming finds the provably best order in O(n^2 2^n) time, which is instant up to about a dozen stops.
  3. Heuristics for comparison and for larger jobs. Nearest-next-stop construction, then 2-opt and Or-opt improvement (re-evaluating whole tours, since reversing a stretch of an asymmetric tour changes its cost).

The first stop is the depot. Tours either return to it or end at the last drop.

docs.title: ridegraph.matching
docs.text:
Assigning drivers to riders.

Given a matrix of pickup times (driver x rider), find the assignment that minimises the total. This is the linear assignment problem; the Hungarian algorithm solves it exactly in O(n^2 m) using dual potentials, here in the compact shortest-augmenting-path form.

Rectangular inputs are fine: with more drivers than riders every rider is matched; with more riders than drivers every driver is. Pairs that must not be matched (pickup too far away) carry FORBIDDEN and are dropped from the result afterwards.

docs.title: ridegraph.eta
docs.text:
Learned ETA: correcting the router's estimate from how trips actually go.

Production ride-hailing systems do not trust the routing engine's ETA as is. The graph knows road speeds, but not the queue that always forms at a particular junction, how long lights really hold you at 8:30, or that the evening peak arrives later than the timetable says. The approach popularised by Uber's DeepETA keeps the routing engine and trains a model to predict the residual: the gap between the engine's ETA and the trip time actually observed, from features of the route and the moment.

Real trip logs for London are not public, so this module also provides the observations: World is a hidden ground truth, a city that differs from the router's model in ways a real one would. It has congestion hotspots, a later and stronger peak, extra slowdown on main roads, waits at turns and lights, occasional incidents and noise. Trips are routed with the router, timed by the world, and models learn the correction from route features alone. They are judged on trips they never saw.

Everything a feature uses is something a production system would know at request time: the route, its geometry and road mix, its manoeuvres and the time. Nothing reads the hidden world.

The model runs in the browser too: the gradient-boosted trees export to JSON and web/js/eta.js computes the same features and walks the same trees.

docs.title: ridegraph.gnn
docs.text:
A graph neural network ETA: learn a slowdown for every road, from trips alone.

The gradient-boosted model (eta.py) sees a route as one row of summary features. A graph neural network instead works on the roads themselves, the way DeepMind's model for Google Maps does: it learns a representation of every road segment from the segment and its neighbourhood in the network, predicts how much slower than the router each segment really is at a given time, and adds the segments of a route up.

Architecture (numpy only, gradients written out by hand):

  • Message passing, precomputed. Each road segment starts with its own features: road class, length, traffic lights, junction size, and its position encoded with sines and cosines. Features are then averaged over the line graph (segments are neighbours when one leads into the other) for 1, 2, 4 and 8 hops with symmetric normalisation, and all hops are concatenated. Precomputing the propagation is the SIGN approach (Frasca et al., 2020): it scales to every road in a city, and a learned network on top decides which hop to trust for each road.
  • A segment network. A two-layer MLP reads a segment's representation together with the time of day and predicts g, the log of its slowdown.
  • A route readout. Predicted time is the sum over the route's segments of router seconds x exp(g), plus a learned wait for each kind of turn and each set of traffic lights, also by time of day.

The loss is the squared error of log(predicted / observed), trained with Adam on minibatches of trips.

docs.title: ridegraph.osrm
docs.text:
A head-to-head with OSRM, the open-source routing engine used in production.

Agreeing with yourself proves little: every algorithm here is tested against Dijkstra, but all of them share this package's map parsing and speed model. OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) shares neither. It parses OpenStreetMap with its own C++ code and routes with Multi-Level Dijkstra, the engine behind many commercial map products.

To compare like with like, OSRM is given the same roads and the same speeds:

  • write_osm_xml writes the ways this package treats as drivable, with their tags, as OSM XML for osrm-extract;
  • write_segment_speeds writes this package's free-flow speed for every road segment as an OSRM segment speed file, which osrm-customize loads in place of OSRM's own speed guesses;
  • the CI workflow switches off OSRM's turn and traffic-light penalties, since the free-flow router here has none.

compare then asks both engines the same random questions and reports how often the travel times agree, how much of the two routes coincide, and how long each takes to answer. Differences that remain come from the parts that are genuinely independent: OSM parsing, which ways each engine accepts, how coordinates snap to roads, and OSRM storing times in tenths of a second.

docs.title: ridegraph.validation
docs.text:
How realistic is the simulated London? A check against published speeds.

The learned ETA is trained and scored on trips timed in a hidden simulated city (eta.World), because real trip data is not available to a personal project. That makes one question unavoidable: are its speeds plausible for central London? This module times random trips in the simulated city at several times of day and sets the results beside independent published figures:

  • Department for Transport, Travel time measures for local 'A' roads, 2022 (tables CGN0503b and CGN0503d): average speed on local A roads in the City of London 7.7 mph and Camden 8.1 mph, the two slowest local authorities in England, and 14.4 mph across Greater London.
  • TomTom Traffic Index 2023: London's city centre averaged about 10 mph, falling to 8.5 mph at peak hours.

The definitions differ (DfT measures A roads only, TomTom whole trips in its own city-centre area), so the comparison is about the range, not a single target.

docs.title: ridegraph.api
docs.text:
An HTTP routing service: the engine behind a JSON API.

The map runs in the browser; a product would also want a backend. This module wraps the package as a FastAPI application:

  • GET /route: the quickest route at any time of day, optionally with alternatives and Congestion Charge avoidance, as GeoJSON, with the learned ETA and its arrival window when a model is loaded.
  • GET /reach: area reachable within some minutes, leaving or arriving.
  • POST /tour: the best order for a round of stops.
  • GET /health: what is loaded.

Any time of day, not just presets. Queries run on a Customizable Contraction Hierarchy (cch.py) built once at start-up. A request for 08:15 loads that quarter-hour's travel times into it, which takes tens of milliseconds, and the result is kept in a small cache, so later requests in the same quarter-hour pay nothing. A plain CH would need seconds of preprocessing per time.

Searches share one hierarchy, so they run under a lock; each takes a few milliseconds, and the service scales by running more worker processes.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
ridegraph is a Python package that does the heavy lifting offline and a static web page that runs the same algorithms in the browser. There is no server: CI builds everything and publishes files.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Offline["Python package (CI or your machine)"]
        OSM[(OpenStreetMap<br/>Overpass API)] --> parse[osm.py<br/>parse and prune]
        parse --> net[RoadNetwork<br/>CSR arrays]
        net --> speeds[speeds.py + traffic.py<br/>seconds per road by time of day]
        speeds --> ch[ch.py<br/>Contraction Hierarchy per preset]
        net --> cch[cch.py<br/>nested dissection + fill-in]
        net --> turns[turns.py<br/>edge-expanded graph]
        ch --> eta[eta.py + gnn.py<br/>simulated trips, trained models]
        ch --> dispatch[demand.py + dispatch.py<br/>simulated mornings]
        TfL[(TfL disruption feed)] --> live[live.py<br/>map matching]
        ch & cch & eta & dispatch & live --> export[web_export.py<br/>binary arrays + JSON]
    end
    subgraph Browser["Static site"]
        export --> engine[engine.js<br/>searches, CH, many-to-many]
        engine --> cchjs[cch.js<br/>customisation]
        engine --> alt[alternatives.js]
        engine --> tour[tour.js]
        engine --> etajs[eta.js<br/>tree walk]

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Data. overpass.py downloads drivable roads with retries and mirror fallback. osm.py keeps the ways a car may use, splits them into one segment per pair of consecutive OSM nodes, respects one-way rules, and keeps the largest strongly connected component so every route can return.

Graph. graph.py stores the network as flat arrays and builds a compressed sparse row (CSR) graph whose edge weights are seconds. speeds.py turns road class and speed limits into free-flow speeds, and traffic.py scales them by time of day and by how sensitive each class of road is to congestion. turns.py builds the edge-expanded graph used for turn and traffic-light costs.

Search. dijkstra.py is the reference. bidirectional.py, astar.py, ch.py (Contraction Hierarchies, with many-to-many) and cch.py (Customizable CH) must all match it, and router.py hides which graph a scenario needs. alternatives.py, reach.py and tour.py build everyday tools on top.

Learning. eta.py simulates trips in a hidden world calibrated to London, extracts route features and trains ridge, MLP, gradient-boosted trees and quantile models with conformal calibration. gnn.py trains the graph neural network over every road. demand.py forecasts ride requests.

Decisions. matching.py holds the Hungarian algorithm. dispatch.py simulates a fleet under six policies on identical requests.

Integration. live.py matches TfL disruptions onto the graph, charges.py holds the Congestion Charge zone, osrm.py prepares the head-to-head with OSRM, and web_export.py writes everything the browser needs.

docs.title: The browser
docs.text: The export is a manifest plus gzipped, 8-byte-aligned binary arrays that the browser views directly as typed arrays, so loading London takes no parsing. engine.js ports every search; cch.js re-customises when live closures arrive; eta.js walks the exported trees; dispatch.js replays the simulation, rebuilding each leg's route with the same hierarchy. Node tests run these modules against Python on the same data and require identical answers.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text: Each entry records a choice, what else was on the table, and why it went this way. The costs are listed too, because every one of these has some.

docs.title: Implement the algorithms instead of calling a library
docs.text:
• Alternatives: NetworkX, OSRM, GraphHopper.
  • Why: the point is to understand where routing speed comes from, and to be able to change anything (turn costs, live times, the browser port).
  • Cost: more code to trust, which is why every method is tested against Dijkstra, property-tested on random graphs, and compared with OSRM.

docs.title: Seconds, not metres, on every edge
docs.text:
• Alternatives: distance with a speed applied afterwards.
  • Why: "quickest" depends on speed, which depends on road class, limits and time of day. Putting seconds on the edges makes every algorithm optimise the right thing with no special cases.
  • Cost: a new set of weights per time of day, and preprocessing per set.

docs.title: Flat CSR arrays and Python lists in hot loops
docs.text:
• Alternatives: an object per node, NetworkX graphs, numpy indexing in loops.
  • Why: CSR is compact, exports to the browser byte for byte, and Python lists are several times faster than numpy scalar access inside a heap loop.
  • Cost: less readable than objects; documented at each array.

docs.title: Both Contraction Hierarchies and Customizable CH
docs.text:
• Alternatives: CH only, or CCH only.
  • Why: CH with witness searches gives the smallest, fastest hierarchy for a fixed set of times (97 junctions settled per query). CCH is larger but its times can be replaced in milliseconds, which is what live closures need. The map uses CH by default and steps over to CCH when live times are on.
  • Cost: two hierarchies to build and test.

docs.title: Geometric nested dissection for CCH
docs.text:
• Alternatives: METIS, KaHIP, inertial flow.
  • Why: no native dependency, and on London a median cut in the best of four directions gives 3.9 times the original edges and 3.2 million triangles, small enough to customise in 20 ms in the browser.
  • Cost: a graph partitioner would give fewer shortcuts; the gap is acceptable at city scale.

docs.title: A browser port instead of a server
docs.text:
• Alternatives: a routing API that the page calls.
  • Why: a static site costs nothing to host, cannot go down, and lets every search be animated junction by junction.
  • Cost: two implementations; Node tests hold the JavaScript to Python on the same exported data.

docs.title: Simulated trips for the learned ETA
docs.text:
• Alternatives: real trip data, which is not available to a personal project.
  • Why: a hidden world with hotspots, a later rush hour and waits at lights and turns, calibrated to London's average speeds, lets the models be scored honestly against a truth they never see, including whether they rediscover the hotspots.
  • Cost: results describe a believable London, not the real one. The writing says so wherever numbers appear.

docs.title: Ship the trees, report the graph neural network
docs.text:
• Alternatives: ship the GNN.
  • Why: the GNN is slightly more accurate (6.6% against 6.8%) but needs a learned representation of every road, about 60 MB, against a few hundred small trees.
  • Cost: the browser shows the second-best model; the model card says so.

docs.title: Calibrate the arrival window with conformal prediction
docs.text:
• Alternatives: raw quantile models.
  • Why: raw 10th and 90th percentile models covered 77% of trips against an 80% target. Conformalized quantile regression widens the window by exactly the margin that restores coverage on held-out data (81%).
  • Cost: a slice of training data held back for calibration.

docs.title: Compare dispatch policies on identical requests
docs.text:
• Alternatives: separate random runs per policy.
  • Why: the same riders, the same fleet and the same willingness to pay make differences between policies attributable to the policy alone.
  • Cost: one simulated morning per policy per day, run in CI.

docs.title: Report surge pricing without supply response
docs.text:
• Alternatives: model extra drivers coming online when prices rise.
  • Why: any supply curve would be an assumption that decides the answer. The simulation isolates rationing and says plainly that this is all it shows.
  • Cost: surge looks worse than its real-world case, which rests on supply.

docs.title: Three cities, one engine
docs.text:
Nothing in the engine is London-specific. ridegraph/cities.py gives each city its area, the places a person would name on the map, where ride demand concentrates and which side of the road traffic drives on; the same pipeline downloads, builds, contracts, trains and simulates each one, and the map switches between them, keeping the view inside the chosen city.

City Area Extras Central London Paddington to Whitechapel, King's Cross to Vauxhall Congestion Charge, live TfL closures, checked against OSRM and published speeds Nicosia The south of the city, stopping short of the buffer zone so no route crosses the Green Line Drives on the left, like London Manhattan Battery to Central Park South, with the bridges to Brooklyn and Queens Drives on the right, so turn costs are mirrored

The time-of-day traffic pattern is London's everywhere; only London's has been checked against real figures.

docs.title: 1. The map is a graph
docs.text:
Intersections become nodes and road segments become directed edges. A two-way street is two edges; a one-way street or roundabout is one.

The pipeline (ridegraph/osm.py) pulls drivable ways from OpenStreetMap, drops what a car cannot use (footpaths, private roads, car park aisles), applies oneway, roundabout and motorway direction rules, then keeps only the largest strongly connected component. That last step matters: cutting a city out of a bounding box leaves stubs you can drive into but never leave, and a router that starts there would fail.

docs.title: 2. Edges cost seconds, not metres
docs.text:
The quickest route is not the shortest one. Each edge's weight is its travel time (ridegraph/speeds.py):

seconds = length / free-flow speed

Free-flow speed comes from the posted maxspeed when OSM has it, discounted to what drivers actually sustain between junctions, or from a typical speed for the road class otherwise. So 900 m of main road can beat 600 m of back street, and the tests check that it does.

The raw map (RoadNetwork) and the weighted routing graph (Graph) are kept separate, so swapping in a traffic model means rebuilding weights, not re-downloading the map. Edges are stored in CSR (compressed sparse row) form, the layout production engines use: all edges leaving node u sit contiguously in head[first_out[u]:first_out[u + 1]], with a mirrored incoming index for searches that run backwards.

docs.title: 3. Four ways to search
docs.text:
Dijkstra (dijkstra.py) grows a ball of settled nodes outward from the start in order of travel time; when the destination is settled, its time is provably optimal. It is the reference every other algorithm must agree with, and its weakness motivates the rest: the ball expands in every direction, including away from the destination.

Bidirectional Dijkstra (bidirectional.py) searches from both ends at once, so two half-size balls replace one big one. The subtle part is the stopping rule: the first node both searches reach is not necessarily on the best route, so the search tracks the best joined route seen and stops only once the two frontiers together cannot beat it.

A* (astar.py) adds a sense of direction by ranking nodes on time so far plus an estimate of time remaining: straight-line distance at the network's top speed. That estimate can never overshoot, so results stay optimal while the search stretches towards the target. In a city the gain is bounded because "top speed in a straight line" is very optimistic.

Contraction Hierarchies (ch.py) is what production routing engines rely on. A one-off preprocessing step ranks nodes by importance and removes them from least to most important. Whenever removing node v would break a quickest route u -> v -> w, a shortcut edge u -> w is added, unless a local witness search finds another route that is just as quick.

Afterwards, every quickest route can be found by searching only upwards in the ranking from both ends, so each query explores a small cone instead of a ball of the city. The implementation includes lazy priority updates during ordering, bounded witness searches, stall-on-demand at query time, and recursive unpacking of shortcuts back into real road segments.

docs.title: 4. Traffic and turns
docs.text:
Rush hour (traffic.py). The same road has a different speed at 3am and 8am. Each edge's speed is scaled by a city-wide congestion curve for the hour (separate weekday and weekend curves) and by how sensitive that class of road is to congestion: arterials lose up to half their speed at the peak, residential streets far less, because through-traffic avoids them. So at 8am the quickest route can leave the main road for back streets, and the tests check that it does. The curves are illustrative, shaped after London's familiar pattern rather than fitted to measured data; production systems use historical and live per-segment speeds from vehicle GPS traces, which would slot in here without touching the routing code.

Turns (turns.py). In a plain road graph, a node is an intersection, so the search cannot tell turning right across oncoming traffic from carrying straight on. The fix is an edge-expanded graph: each node is a directed road segment ("I just drove u to v") and each edge is a manoeuvre ("then take v to w"), costing the next segment's travel time plus a turn penalty. UK defaults make right turns (crossing traffic) dearer than left turns, with extra cost for sharp turns, U-turns and traffic lights parsed from OSM. A bend in a single road is not a junction, so it costs nothing.

Every algorithm runs on the expanded graph unchanged, Contraction Hierarchies included, since it is just another weighted graph. A Router (router.py) builds the right graph for a scenario and maps routes back to intersections.

$ python -m ridegraph eta <from> <to> --turns
03:00 weekday, with turn costs    2 min 20 s   1.01 km  reference route
08:00 weekday, with turn costs    3 min 59 s   0.99 km  different route (30% shared)
13:00 weekday, with turn costs    3 min 06 s   1.01 km  same route
17:30 weekday, with turn costs    3 min 50 s   0.99 km  different route (30% shared)

Synthetic street grid; London output lands with the next data refresh.

docs.title: 5. Live closures and Customizable Contraction Hierarchies
docs.text:
Contraction Hierarchies are fast because they are built for one set of travel times. A closure on Oxford Street makes them stale, and rebuilding takes far longer than a user will wait. Production engines (OSRM's MLD, Bing Maps) separate the road layout from the times. ridegraph/cch.py implements Customizable CH (Dibbelt, Strasser and Wagner, 2016):

  1. Once per map: order junctions by nested dissection (cut the city along the direction that crosses the fewest roads, recurse on each half, rank the separator last), then contract in that order adding every shortcut, with no witness searches. On London: 77,124 roads become 301,179 edges and 3.19 million lower triangles, in 8 s.
  2. Whenever times change: load the current time of every road and sweep the triangles bottom-up, u->w = min(u->w, u->v + v->w). That takes 50 ms in numpy and about 20 ms in the browser.
  3. Queries: the usual two upward searches, with shortcuts unpacked through the triangles.

The times come from Transport for London's open disruption feed (ridegraph/live.py). Each disrupted stretch is map-matched onto the graph (both ends and the middle of an edge within 18 m of the line). Closed roads get an infinite time, and open ones are slowed by severity. The map asks TfL directly when you switch on Live roadworks and closures. If the feed can't be reached from the browser, it falls back to a snapshot taken when CI built the page.

python -m ridegraph live                      # what is disrupted right now
python -m ridegraph route 51.5130,-0.1590 51.5160,-0.1300 --at 13:00 --live

docs.title: 6. Alternative routes and the Congestion Charge
docs.text:
Map apps offer two or three routes because the quickest is not always the one you want. ridegraph/alternatives.py finds them with the penalty method: take the quickest route, make every road on it 40% slower, search again, and repeat. Each search is pushed off the corridor already used. A candidate is kept only if it is

  • at most 30% slower than the quickest (on real times, not penalised ones),
  • at most 65% shared with any route already offered, and
  • free of pointless detours: sampled stretches of a quarter of the trip must each be within 15% of the quickest way between their ends.

Closing roads is the same machinery with infinite penalties, which is how a route avoids the Congestion Charge zone (ridegraph/charges.py: the zone polygon, £18 a day, 07:00 to 18:00 on weekdays and 12:00 to 18:00 at weekends; the boundary roads are free). From Paddington to Aldgate at 8am:

Route Time Charge Quickest 36 min 32 s £18 Alternative 1 40 min 11 s £18 Alternative 2 45 min 27 s £18 Avoiding the zone, along Euston Road and City Road 50 min 08 s none

So staying out of the zone costs 14 minutes on this trip, about £1.30 a minute saved. The browser runs the same method (A* on the penalised weights, under 100 ms on London) and a Node test holds it to Python.

python -m ridegraph route 51.5265,-0.1820 51.5100,-0.0700 --at 08:00 --alternatives --avoid-charge

docs.title: 7. The learned ETA
docs.text:
The router's estimate is only as good as its model of road speeds. It cannot know that lights on a particular corridor hold you for half a minute at 8:30, that one junction always queues, or that the evening peak arrives later than the timetable. Production ride-hailing systems therefore keep the routing engine and learn the residual: given a route and a moment, how far off will the engine be? ridegraph/eta.py follows that design.

Features are things a production system knows when the trip is requested: the router's ETA, route length, straight-line distance and detour, the share of the route on main roads, B roads and side streets, the number of left, right, sharp and U-turns and of traffic lights on the route, time of day (as a point on a circle, so 23:59 sits next to 00:00), weekday or weekend, and where the route starts, ends and passes through.

The target is log(observed time / router ETA), so the model learns a multiplicative correction and large and small trips weigh evenly.

Observed trips. Real trip logs for London are not public, so the pipeline generates them, and it is open about it. A World is a hidden ground truth that differs from the router the way a real city would: congestion hotspots around a few busy junctions, a rush hour that peaks later and harder than the router assumes, main roads that clog more than modelled, waits at right turns and traffic lights that grow with traffic, occasional incidents and day-to-day noise. 20,000 trips between random points at random times are routed with Contraction Hierarchies and timed in that world. Nothing in the features reads the world directly; the models have to infer its effects from routes and outcomes.

Results are measured on 4,000 trips the models never saw:

Model Mean abs. error 90th pct. error Within 10% Router alone 27.5% 38.5% 2% Router times one global factor 10.1% 20.3% 58% Ridge regression 7.6% 15.5% 74% Neural network (MLP, 64x64) 7.3% 14.4% 75% Gradient-boosted trees (shipped to the map) 6.8% 13.8% 78% Graph neural network over every road 6.6% 13.4% 80%

The simulated city is calibrated to central London: trips average about 21 km/h at night, 14 at midday and 11 at the peaks. The router alone is optimistic by about 28%, mostly because it knows nothing about traffic lights or about when the peaks really arrive. Time of day is the model's most useful signal, followed by where the route runs, weekday or weekend, length and the number of sets of lights. One global factor helps, a linear model helps more, and both non-linear models capture the interactions (lights cost more at peak; hotspots matter only when the route passes through them). Gradient-boosted trees win among the models that read one row per trip and, being a few hundred small trees, are also the easiest to ship.

A graph neural network (ridegraph/gnn.py) works on the roads instead of on trip summaries, the approach DeepMind took for Google Maps. Every road segment starts with its own features (class, length, lights, junction size, position as sines and cosines), which are then averaged over the line graph (segments that lead into one another) for 1, 2, 4 and 8 hops. That is SIGN-style message passing, precomputed so it scales to all 127,000 segments. A two-layer network reads each segment's representation and the time of day and predicts its slowdown; a trip's time is the sum of router seconds x slowdown over its segments plus learned waits for each turn and set of lights. It is written in numpy with hand-derived gradients (checked against finite differences in the tests) and trained with Adam.

On held-out London trips it edges out the trees: 6.6% error against 6.8%, 80% of trips within 10% against 78%. The trees still run in the browser, since the network needs the representation of every road (about 60 MB). The network's per-road slowdowns at 08:30 correlate at r = 0.60 with the hidden truth road by road, a harder test than the trees' area map below.

Traffic lights in OpenStreetMap are often tagged on each approach to a junction and on nearby crossings, about 10 points per km of central London route. Signal nodes within 60 m along a route therefore count as one set (about 4 per km), both in the simulation and in the model's features.

Arrival windows. A single number hides how much trips vary, so two more gradient-boosted models predict the 10th and 90th percentiles, and each trip gets a range such as "usually 25 to 36 min". Quantile models alone tend to be overconfident (77% coverage on London against an 80% target), so the window is calibrated with conformalized quantile regression: part of the training set is held back, the models' misses on it are measured, and the window is widened by exactly the margin that gives 80% coverage on new trips. On held-out London trips it lands at 81.0%, with misses split evenly above and below.

What the model learned. The hidden hotspots are never shown to the model, yet it should find them, since trips through them run slow. The map's Learned slowdown layer asks the model how far off the router a typical trip through each grid square would be at the chosen time, and shades the square accordingly. Against the hidden hotspot field this map correlates at r = 0.83 on London (0.91 on a synthetic grid): the model has located the congestion from trip outcomes alone.

How realistic is the simulated city? python -m ridegraph validate times random weekday trips (about 6 km) in it and sets the speeds beside published figures:

Weekday time Simulated trips Router's estimate 03:00 20.9 km/h 25.4 km/h 08:00 11.1 km/h 16.2 km/h 13:00 13.7 km/h 19.6 km/h 17:30 10.9 km/h 16.8 km/h Published figure Source Speed City of London, local A roads DfT 2022 (CGN0503d) 12.4 km/h Camden, local A roads DfT 2022 (CGN0503d) 13.0 km/h London city centre, all day TomTom Traffic Index 2023 16.1 km/h London city centre, peak hours TomTom Traffic Index 2023 13.7 km/h

Midday in the simulated city (13.7 km/h) sits right among the official figures for the boroughs it covers, and the router's own daytime estimate (16 to 20 km/h) is close to TomTom's all-day figure, which is what a router that knows nothing about lights or queues should look like. The simulated rush hours run about 20% slower than TomTom's peak figure, so if anything the models are trained and tested on a harsher London than the real one. The definitions differ (DfT counts A roads only, TomTom whole trips in its own city-centre area), so these are a range to sit within, not a target to fit.

In the browser. The trees export to JSON, and web/js/eta.js computes the same features and walks the same trees. A test runs it under Node and requires its features and predictions to match Python's to nine decimal places.

docs.title: 8. Travel-time maps and delivery rounds
docs.text:
Travel-time maps (ridegraph/reach.py) answer "where can I get to in 20 minutes from here?", or, for someone choosing where to live, "from where can I get to my office in 20 minutes?". It is a single-source search that settles junctions in time order and stops at the budget, run on the reverse graph for journeys into a point. Reachable area is counted over 250 m squares. From Holborn, 10 minutes reaches 12.2 km² at 08:00 against 36.6 km² at 03:00: rush hour shrinks a 10-minute radius to a third.

Delivery rounds (ridegraph/tour.py) find the best order to visit a list of stops, the travelling salesman problem on one-way streets, where A to B and B to A take different times:

  1. One many-to-many Contraction Hierarchies query prices every stop against every other at the chosen time of day.
  2. Held-Karp dynamic programming finds the provably best order, instant up to about a dozen stops.
  3. Nearest-next-stop construction plus 2-opt and Or-opt improvement give a fast heuristic for comparison and for larger jobs, re-costing whole tours on each move because reversing a stretch of an asymmetric tour changes its cost.
Eight drops from Holborn, midday, round trip Time In the order entered 2 h 07 min Nearest next stop 1 h 20 min Nearest next stop + 2-opt/Or-opt 1 h 05 min Optimal (Held-Karp) 1 h 05 min 
python -m ridegraph reach 51.5174,-0.1200 --at 08:00
python -m ridegraph tour 51.5174,-0.1200 51.5308,-0.1238 51.5033,-0.1145 ...

docs.title: 9. Ride dispatch and demand forecasting
docs.text:
Routing exists to answer a business question: which driver should take this ride? ridegraph/dispatch.py simulates a fleet over the 07:00 to 10:00 morning peak and compares six ways of answering it, on exactly the same ride requests and the same starting fleet.

Demand (ridegraph/demand.py) comes from places with their own rhythm: main-line stations busy at commuting hours, the City and Holborn filling in the morning and emptying in the evening, Soho, Covent Garden and Shoreditch at night, plus requests from anywhere. Every day has its own level, its own surprises at each hotspot, and a couple of unannounced events (a match, a concert) that make one area surge for an hour or two.

Pricing every pairing at once. Every 30 seconds the dispatcher needs the pickup time from every free driver to every waiting rider. Running one query per pair would be hundreds of searches; bucket-based many-to-many Contraction Hierarchies do it with one small upward search per driver and per rider, then join them through buckets at the nodes they share.

The methods compared:

  • Nearest driver. Riders, oldest first, each take the closest free driver.
  • Optimal matching. The Hungarian algorithm (ridegraph/matching.py) assigns the whole batch at once to minimise total pickup time, with each rider's cost reduced by how long they have already waited so that hard-to-reach riders are not left until they give up.
  • Optimal + repositioning. Idle drivers also move towards neighbourhoods where expected demand over the next 15 minutes most exceeds the drivers already there, using either the historical average for that place and time, or an ML demand forecast.
  • + shared rides. The forecast method, and riders going the same way share a car. A waiting rider can join a car already carrying one rider: the car's position is the last junction it has reached on its route (every prefix of a quickest route is itself quickest, so a binary search over CH queries finds it), and every pickup and drop order is priced. Riders in the same batch can also pair up from the start. Nobody is held up by more than 40% of their own trip or six minutes, and the pairs that save most driving go first.
  • + surge pricing. The forecast method, and every two minutes each neighbourhood gets a price multiplier from how far waiting and expected riders outnumber nearby free drivers. Each rider accepts with probability exp(-(multiplier - 1)), and idle drivers are drawn towards surging areas. Surge here does not bring extra drivers online, so the comparison isolates its rationing effect.

The forecast is a gradient-boosted Poisson model predicting ride requests per 500 m square for the next 15 minutes, from the time, the place and what has happened so far today (the last 15 minutes and the last hour, nearby and city-wide). On days it never saw:

Forecast Poisson deviance (lower is better) Same as the last 15 minutes 3.35 Historical average for the time 0.77 Gradient-boosted forecast 0.39

Results, averaged over 6 simulated London mornings with 115 drivers:

Method Avg. wait 90th pct. wait Pickup drive Gave up Empty driving per driver Nearest driver 7.3 min 13.3 min 5.8 min 5.9% 0 Optimal matching 6.6 min 12.1 min 5.4 min 6.2% 0 Optimal + historical-average repositioning 6.2 min 11.6 min 5.1 min 4.9% 16 min Optimal + ML-forecast repositioning 6.1 min 11.3 min 4.9 min 5.0% 12 min + shared rides 5.1 min 9.6 min 4.4 min 1.4% 14 min + surge pricing 5.2 min 9.6 min 4.7 min 0.3% 14 min

Optimal matching alone cuts waits by about 10%, and repositioning ahead of demand brings the total to 16%. The ML forecast halves the forecasting error of the historical average, but in this dispatch loop that shows up mainly as efficiency: it reaches the best waits while sending drivers on about a quarter less empty repositioning, because it moves them only where demand is actually building today. Better forecasts do not automatically mean proportionally better decisions; the repositioning rule is where the next gains would come from.

The two product levers pull in opposite directions:

On top of the ML-forecast method Riders served Shared Priced out Fleet driving per ride served Neither 95.0% none none 25.7 min Shared rides 98.6% 46% of rides none 22.1 min Surge pricing 91.3% none 8.5% 25.8 min

Shared rides serve more people with less driving: 46% of rides are shared, waits fall by 16%, those who give up drop from 5.0% to 1.4%, and the fleet drives 14% less per rider served. The price is 2.1 extra minutes in the car for a shared rider. Surge pricing also shortens waits (5.2 min, almost nobody gives up), but by turning riders away: 8.5% decline the price, so fewer riders are served than with no surge at all. Without the extra drivers a higher price draws in, surge only rations a fixed fleet. That is the honest reading of the simulation, and the reason real platforms justify surge by its effect on supply.

docs.title: 10. The live map
docs.text:
The demo in web/ runs entirely in the browser, with no server:

  • Same data, same answers. python -m ridegraph export-web writes the graph and one Contraction Hierarchy per time-of-day preset as compact, gzipped binary arrays. web/js/engine.js is a direct port of the algorithms, and a test runs it under Node and requires exact agreement with the Python router on every preset.
  • The map is the graph. Rather than a tile server's picture of London, the page draws the very network being searched, styled like a street atlas: roads coloured by class, the Thames, and a lettered grid so routes read as "5C to 9I".
  • Search you can see. Every settled junction lights up its streets in the colour of the side that reached it, so Dijkstra visibly floods the city while Contraction Hierarchies touches a few hundred junctions scattered up the road hierarchy. All five methods (Customizable CH included) run on every trip, with junctions examined and query time side by side.
  • Routes, charges and closures. Each trip lists the quickest route and up to two alternatives with their times and whether they enter the Congestion Charge zone, which is drawn on the map; a switch adds the quickest route that stays out. Live roadworks and closures asks TfL's feed directly, draws the closed streets and re-customises the hierarchy, while plain CH steps aside because its shortcuts are stale.
  • Turn costs on demand. A switch charges for turns and traffic lights. The browser rebuilds the edge-expanded turn graph from per-manoeuvre turn kinds in the export, numbered exactly as the Python one, and the trip summary lists the right and left turns, U-turns and lights on the route. Contraction Hierarchies are switched off in this mode: an edge-based hierarchy for London would add around 20 MB per time of day, so turn-aware hierarchies live in the Python tool instead.
  • Learned ETA beside the router's. Every trip shows both estimates and a calibrated arrival window; a model card gives each model's error on held-out trips and the features the model leans on, and a map layer shades the city by the slowdown the model learned for the chosen time.
  • Four modes. Plan a route, Travel-time map (click anywhere; leaving or arriving; each band compared with 3am), Deliveries (click to add up to 12 stops; every ordering method compared, the best drawn and numbered) and Dispatch rides. The browser runs the same algorithms as Python, held to them by Node tests.
  • Dispatch you can watch. A Dispatch rides mode replays a simulated morning: cars coloured by what they are doing (orange when carrying two riders) move along their real routes, riders wait and are collected, surge squares show their multipliers, and every method's running averages update side by side. Only the decisions are stored; the browser rebuilds every route with the same hierarchy, and a test holds each leg to the duration the simulation recorded.
  • Built and deployed by CI. On each push, a workflow downloads central London from OpenStreetMap (cached between runs), snapshots TfL's disruptions, builds the graph, contracts it for each preset, trains the ETA models, simulates dispatch and publishes web/ to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: 11. An HTTP API
docs.text:
The map needs no server, but a product would. ridegraph/api.py serves the engine as a FastAPI application with OpenAPI docs at /docs:

Endpoint Answers GET /route?from=lat,lon&to=lat,lon&at=08:15 The quickest route as GeoJSON, with distance, Congestion Charge and the learned ETA with its arrival window; alternatives=2 and avoid_charge=true add more routes GET /reach?from=lat,lon&minutes=10,20,30&arriving=false Area reachable within each time POST /tour Best visiting order for up to 13 stops, every method compared GET /health What is loaded

Any minute of the day. The browser offers four preset times because each plain hierarchy is built for one set of travel times. The API answers for any time by keeping one Customizable CH and loading each quarter-hour's times into it on first use (tens of milliseconds), with recent quarter-hours cached, including the plain-list views the search loop reads.

Measured with scripts/loadtest.py on central London, one worker, on a 2-vCPU machine that also ran the load generator: 14 ms median and 21 ms 95th-percentile latency for a route with its learned ETA, about 70 requests a second per worker, no errors over 2,000 random requests spread over six quarter-hours. Start-up, including building the hierarchy, takes 9 s. More throughput is more workers.

pip install -e ".[api,ml]"
python -m ridegraph serve --eta-model web/data/eta-model.json
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8000/route?from=51.5154,-0.1410&to=51.5033,-0.1145&at=08:15"

docker build -t ridegraph . && docker run -p 8000:8000 ridegraph

A CI workflow builds the image and checks the running container answers.

docs.title: 12. What the London numbers show
docs.text:
• Contraction Hierarchies work because real roads are hierarchical. On a uniform synthetic grid the reduction in search work is 24x; on London it is 389x, with preprocessing adding fewer shortcuts (121k) than the map has road segments. Main roads naturally end up at the top of the ranking.
  • A* barely helps in a city. Its estimate assumes the fastest road speed in a straight line, but London's average route speed is about half of that, so the search still covers a wide ellipse. This is why production engines rely on preprocessing rather than on geometric heuristics.
  • Bidirectional search halves the work in theory but not the time in Python, because juggling two frontiers costs interpreter overhead that eats most of the saving.

docs.title: 13. Measuring fairly
docs.text:
Benchmarks report nodes settled alongside wall-clock time. Settled nodes measure the work each algorithm does, independent of language; Python timings mostly measure interpreter overhead per node, which is why Contraction Hierarchies' 24x reduction in work shows up as a smaller time gain here. Every benchmark query is also cross-checked against Dijkstra, so a benchmark run doubles as a correctness check.

Against OSRM. Agreeing with Dijkstra proves the searches are right, but they all share this package's map parsing and speed model. OSRM shares neither: it parses OpenStreetMap with its own C++ code and routes with Multi-Level Dijkstra. The Compare with OSRM workflow (ridegraph/osrm.py) gives OSRM v5.27 the ways this package treats as drivable, loads ridegraph's free-flow speed for every one of the 127,286 road segments as a segment speed file, switches off OSRM's turn and traffic-light penalties (the free-flow router has none) and asks both engines the same 1,000 random trips:

ridegraph vs OSRM, 1,000 random central London trips Travel time within 1% of OSRM's 83.7% Travel time within 5% of OSRM's 96.9% Median time difference 0.23% Same route (95%+ of junctions shared) 75.0% Median share of junctions in common 99.7% Median query, ridegraph CH in Python 1.02 ms Median query, OSRM over local HTTP 1.56 ms

What remains comes from the parts that are genuinely independent. OSRM snaps a coordinate to the nearest point on a road rather than to a junction, stores each segment's time in tenths of a second, and applies its own rules about which ways a car may use. Where the routes differ but the times agree, the two engines have found different routes that are equally quick. The query times are not a like-for-like contest (OSRM's include an HTTP round trip), but they show the Python hierarchy is in the same league as a production C++ engine on a city of this size.

docs.title: Road rules and driving behaviour
docs.text:
A route is only useful if a driver can legally follow it, and an arrival time is only useful if it reflects how people actually drive. This page sets out the rules and behaviours that matter for a ride-hailing or delivery router in a city like London, what Ridegraph models today, what it does not model yet, and how each would fit into the engine.

Two kinds of rule are kept apart throughout. Legal rules decide whether a route is allowed at all, so they belong in the road graph: a banned turn is removed, not made expensive. Driving behaviour decides how long a legal route takes or how pleasant it is, so it belongs in the costs: a right turn across traffic is allowed, but it takes longer.

Rule Kind In Ridegraph today One-way streets, roads closed to cars Legal Yes Speed limits Legal Yes, from OpenStreetMap where tagged Live closures and roadworks Legal Yes, from TfL's feed (London) Congestion Charge Legal (a charge) Yes, priced and avoidable Turn restrictions Legal Not yet Bus lanes and bus gates Legal Not yet Time-limited restrictions Legal Not yet ULEZ Legal (a charge) Not yet Where a car may stop Legal Not yet Turning across traffic Behaviour Yes, as a time cost Waiting at traffic lights Behaviour Yes, as one average wait Kerbside pickup Behaviour Not yet Time spent at each stop Behaviour Not yet

docs.title: Turn restrictions
docs.text:
Signs such as "No right turn", "No U-turn" and "Only straight on" are recorded in OpenStreetMap as restriction relations: a road you arrive on, the junction (or short stretch of road) you pass through, and a road you may not, or must, leave by. Central London has thousands of them.

Ridegraph does not read these yet, which means some of its routes may use a turn that a driver is not allowed to make. This is the most important gap on this page, because it affects whether a route is correct rather than how long it takes.

They fit naturally into the turn-aware graph Ridegraph already builds for turn costs (turns.py). In that graph every road segment is a node and every possible move from one segment to the next is an edge, so a "no right turn" is simply an edge that is never created, and an "only straight on" removes every other edge leaving that segment. Restrictions that span several junctions ("via ways") need the same idea applied to short chains of segments. A plain junction-to-junction graph cannot express a turn ban at all, which is one more reason the turn-aware graph is the right one for real routing.

docs.title: Bus lanes and bus gates
docs.text:
Many London streets have lanes, or whole short sections, reserved for buses during some or all of the day. London's licensed black cabs may use most bus lanes; private hire cars, the category Uber drivers fall into, may not. The same journey can therefore have different quickest routes, and different times, depending on the vehicle.

The clean way to model this is with vehicle profiles: one road graph, and a small table saying which roads and lanes each vehicle type may use and when. OpenStreetMap tags bus lanes and bus-only roads (busway, bus:lanes, access=no with psv=yes), so a taxi profile and a private hire profile could be compared on the same trip.

docs.title: Time-limited restrictions
docs.text:
Some rules depend on the clock. School streets close to traffic around the start and end of the school day, some low-traffic neighbourhoods are filtered only at certain times, and "no entry except for access" roads are legal only if your trip starts or ends on them.

Ridegraph already prices travel by time of day, and its Customizable Contraction Hierarchies can load a new set of travel times in about 20 ms, so a time-limited closure can be applied in the same way as a live closure: set the affected roads to impassable for the hours the rule applies and re-customise. Access-only roads need a different treatment, allowing them only as the first or last part of a route.

docs.title: Charges and zones
docs.text: The Congestion Charge is modelled: routes can be priced, and a route that stays out of the zone can be requested. The Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) now covers the whole of Greater London and charges older, more polluting vehicles each day they drive in it. Most ride-hailing cars meet its standard, so it is better treated as a property of the vehicle profile than of the route: a non-compliant vehicle pays it on any London trip.

docs.title: Speed limits
docs.text: Much of central London now has a 20 mph limit: the City of London, boroughs such as Camden and Islington, and the main TfL roads within the Congestion Charge zone. Ridegraph reads the posted limit from OpenStreetMap where it is tagged and assumes traffic flows somewhat below it; where a road has no limit tagged, it falls back on a typical speed for that class of road. The estimate is only as good as the tagging, so the fallback matters most on minor streets.

docs.title: Where a car may stop
docs.text:
A pickup point is only useful if a driver may legally stop there. Red routes (major roads marked with red lines and managed by TfL) restrict stopping, as do double red lines, bus stops and zig-zag markings near crossings. A good pickup point is a short walk from the rider on a street where stopping is allowed, not the exact point they tapped.

Ridegraph currently snaps a pickup to the nearest junction. Choosing legal stopping points needs kerb data that OpenStreetMap only partly records, so this is the hardest item here to do well.

docs.title: Turning across traffic
docs.text:
Turning across oncoming traffic, right in the UK and left in most of the world, means waiting for a gap. It is slower, more likely to cause a collision and wastes fuel while idling. UPS is well known for planning its delivery routes to avoid these turns where it can.

Ridegraph's turn costs already reflect this: in the UK a right turn costs more than a left, a sharp turn more again, and the costs swap sides for cities that drive on the right (Manhattan). A delivery-van profile could go further and make right turns so expensive that they are only used when there is no reasonable alternative.

docs.title: Kerbside pickup
docs.text:
When a rider is waiting on one side of a busy road, a car that arrives on the other side forces them to cross, or forces the driver into a U-turn. Uber and other ride-hailing apps try to send the driver to the rider's side of the road. In routing research this is known as the curb approach: a stop is not just a place but a place and a side, and the vehicle must arrive travelling in the direction that puts the kerb next to it.

To model it, a pickup becomes a point on a directed road segment rather than a junction. In the UK the rider should be on the car's left, so only one direction of travel along that segment is acceptable. The search then has to reach that segment from the right end, which can add a minute or two to the pickup but saves the rider a crossing. The dispatch simulator could then report how much extra driving kerbside pickups cost the fleet, and what it saves riders.

docs.title: Waiting at traffic lights
docs.text:
Ridegraph adds the same average wait, 12 seconds, at every set of traffic lights. Real waits depend on the signal's cycle length, how much of the cycle is green for your direction, and how busy the junction is. Webster's formula, a classic result from traffic engineering, estimates the average delay from exactly those three things, and rises steeply as a junction approaches capacity.

Signal timings are not public for most junctions, but the formula would still let the wait grow at peak times and on busier roads instead of staying flat. The learned arrival-time model already corrects part of this from data: the number of traffic lights on a route is one of its most useful features.

docs.title: Time spent at each stop
docs.text: Every pickup and drop-off takes time: pulling in, the rider getting in or out, luggage, payment. For a single ride it is small; for a delivery round with a dozen stops, or a shared ride that picks up twice, it adds up. A fixed allowance of one to two minutes per stop is a common starting point. Neither the dispatch simulator nor the delivery planner includes it yet: pickups and drop-offs are instant, so their totals are driving time only.

docs.title: Order of work
docs.text:
1. Turn restrictions, because without them a route can be illegal.
  2. Kerbside pickup, because it is the most distinctive ride-hailing problem here and changes what the dispatch results mean.
  3. Vehicle profiles (taxi, private hire, delivery van), which bring bus lanes, ULEZ and stronger turn avoidance in together.
  4. Time-limited restrictions, using the same mechanism as live closures.
  5. Signal delays and stop times, which refine the arrival-time estimates.

docs.title: Rebuilding a ride-hailing routing stack on London's roads
docs.text:
What I learned implementing quickest routes, live closures, learned arrival times and ride dispatch from first principles, and what the numbers say.

Every ride-hailing or maps app answers the same two questions millions of times a second: what is the quickest way from A to B, and when will I get there? Behind them sits a third, the one the business runs on: which driver should take this ride? I built all three from scratch on OpenStreetMap's map of central London (72,637 junctions, 127,286 road segments) to see where the real difficulty lies. Everything is in the repository, and the live map runs the same algorithms in the browser.

docs.title: 1. Fast routes come from preprocessing, not cleverness at query time
docs.text:
Dijkstra's algorithm settles 37,822 junctions on an average London query. A*, the textbook improvement, still settles 23,705: its straight-line estimate assumes the fastest road speed, and London's routes run at about half of it. Contraction Hierarchies settle 97, a 389-fold reduction, because they move the work to preprocessing: junctions are ranked by importance and shortcuts added so every query climbs from each end towards main roads and meets in the middle. The gain is far larger on London than on a uniform grid (24-fold), because real roads are hierarchical. That is the whole idea.

To check the engine against something it did not write itself, CI runs OSRM, the open-source engine behind many commercial maps, on the same roads and speeds. On 1,000 random trips the travel times agree within 1% for 84% of trips (median difference 0.23%), and the routes share a median 99.7% of their junctions. The differences left come from independent map parsing and from how each engine snaps a coordinate to the road.

docs.title: 2. Live traffic needs the layout and the times kept apart
docs.text: A Contraction Hierarchy is built for one set of travel times. A closure on Oxford Street makes it stale, and rebuilding takes seconds. Customizable Contraction Hierarchies split the work: the road layout is ordered once by nested dissection (cut the city along the line that crosses fewest roads, recurse, rank the cut last) and contracted with every possible shortcut. New times are then loaded by sweeping 3.2 million "lower triangles" bottom-up, which takes 50 ms in numpy and about 20 ms in the browser. The map fetches Transport for London's live closures, matches them onto the graph, re-customises and routes around them. Nothing about the query changes; only the cost of keeping it current does.

docs.title: 3. A good alternative route is a constrained search problem
docs.text: Showing a second route sounds trivial until it is a pointless detour or 95% the same road. The penalty method (make the roads on each route found 40% slower, search again) finds candidates; the rules decide which to keep: at most 30% slower, at most 65% shared, and no stretch more than 15% slower than the quickest way between its ends. Closing every road into the Congestion Charge zone is the same machinery with infinite penalties. From Paddington to Aldgate at 8am, staying out of the zone costs 14 minutes and saves £18.

docs.title: 4. Machine learning should correct the router, not replace it
docs.text:
Uber's DeepETA keeps the routing engine and learns its error. I did the same on simulated trips through a city calibrated to London (about 21 km/h at night, 11 at the peaks) that hides congestion hotspots, a later rush hour and waits at lights and turns. On 4,000 held-out trips:

Model Mean error Within 10% Router alone 27.5% 2% Router x one global factor 10.1% 58% Gradient-boosted trees on route features 6.8% 78% Graph neural network over every road 6.6% 80%

Is the simulated city believable? Timed trips run at 13.7 km/h at midday, right among the Department for Transport's 2022 figures for the City of London (12.4 km/h) and Camden (13.0 km/h), while its rush hours (about 11 km/h) are around 20% slower than TomTom's 2023 peak figure for central London. If anything, the models learn on a harsher London than the real one.

Three things stood out. Time of day and the number of sets of traffic lights matter more than distance. Arrival windows need calibration: quantile models alone covered 77% of trips against an 80% target, and conformal calibration brought that to 81%. And the models genuinely discover what they are not shown: the trees' map of slow areas correlates at r = 0.83 with the hidden hotspots. The graph neural network, written in numpy with gradients derived by hand, learns a slowdown for every road segment from its place in the network and is slightly more accurate, but the trees are what ships to the browser: a few hundred small trees against a representation of every road.

docs.title: 5. In dispatch, the decision rule matters more than the forecast
docs.text:
The dispatch simulator replays the same morning of ride requests and the same fleet under each policy. Every 30 seconds one many-to-many query prices every free driver against every waiting rider.

Policy (6 simulated mornings, 115 drivers) Avg. wait Gave up Riders served Driving per ride Nearest free driver 7.3 min 5.9% 94.1% 23.8 min Optimal matching (Hungarian algorithm) 6.6 min 6.2% 93.8% 23.4 min + repositioning on the ML demand forecast 6.1 min 5.0% 95.0% 25.7 min + shared rides 5.1 min 1.4% 98.6% 22.1 min + surge pricing (instead of sharing) 5.2 min 0.3% 91.3% 25.8 min

Optimal matching beats "nearest driver" by about 10% on waits, and moving idle drivers ahead of predicted demand takes the gain to 16%. The demand model halves the forecasting error of a historical average, yet its dispatch gain over that average is small; it mostly shows up as a quarter less empty repositioning. Better predictions do not automatically make proportionally better decisions.

The two product levers were the most interesting result. Shared rides serve more people with less driving: almost half of rides are shared, fewer riders give up, and the fleet drives 14% less per rider served, for about two extra minutes in the car. Surge pricing also shortens waits, but by turning 8.5% of riders away, so fewer are served than with no surge at all. With a fixed fleet, surge only rations; its case rests on the extra drivers a higher price brings out, which is exactly what a simulation like this has to model before it can say anything about surge.
